pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Fair testing — using results to predict and re-test

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use "test results to make predictions to set up further comparative and fair tests" (verbatim), alongside "reporting and presenting findings from enquiries, including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations". This is the point where an enquiry stops being a one-off and becomes an iterative line of enquiry.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 + SEP 4, grades 3–5):** SEP 3 at 3–5 covers planning fair tests with controlled variables; SEP 4 (Analyzing & Interpreting Data) at 3–5 adds "use data to evaluate and refine design solutions" and comparing/contrasting data to make sense of a phenomenon. Using results to generate a testable prediction and a follow-up investigation bridges these two practices.

- **Operational details:** Builds on drawing conclusions and making predictions (prerequisite mt_7VrR1GzhrN) and independently planning enquiries with variable control (prerequisite mt_ArVBEpMAPk); soft-linked to the reasoning habit of describing a pattern as a rule and testing it in new cases (mt_hbe_kdE_7C). The distinctive skill is EXTRAPOLATION-AND-TEST: reading the trend in one set of results, using it to make a specific prediction for a NEW value or condition ('if thinner wire conducted better, an even thinner one should conduct better still'), then designing a fresh fair test to check that prediction. The reasoning link (why the results imply the prediction) must be made explicit. Feeds forward to presenting findings with causal explanations (dependent mt_nyPMkeHlVJ).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can read a trend in results, turn it into a specific testable prediction for a new value, design a follow-up fair test to check it, and articulate the reasoning connecting the original data to the new prediction has met the bar.
bestPractices: Teach prediction as reading the trend, not guessing: pupils point to the pattern in the existing results ('as X increased, Y increased') and extend it to a new, unmeasured value — the prediction is evidence-based, not a hunch.
Distinguish interpolation (a value between tested points) from extrapolation (beyond them) and flag that extrapolated predictions are less certain and precisely why they must be TESTED, not assumed.
Make the reasoning link explicit and spoken/written: 'I predict… BECAUSE the results showed…' — the justification is the assessed skill, not just the prediction itself.
Design the follow-up as a genuine fair test in its own right (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings) so the new question is answered validly.
Model science as an iterative cycle — results raise the next question — rather than a single linear experiment that 'finishes' at a conclusion.
keyRepresentations: A results table/graph with the trend arrow extended to a predicted new value (interpolation vs extrapolation marked)
The sentence frame 'I predict ___ because the results showed ___'
An enquiry cycle: question → fair test → results → prediction → new fair test
A line graph where pupils extend the line of best fit to read off a prediction
A prediction-then-test comparison card (predicted value vs measured value)
commonMisconceptions: Making a prediction as a random guess rather than reading it off the existing trend in the data.
Treating an extrapolated prediction as a proven fact instead of a claim that still needs its own fair test.
Assuming a pattern continues indefinitely beyond the tested range (e.g. that a trend never levels off or reverses) without checking.
Skipping the reasoning link — stating a prediction without connecting it to the specific results that motivate it.
Believing an experiment 'ends' at its conclusion, rather than that good results generate the next testable question.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach the extrapolation-and-test cycle in fair testing: read the trend in an existing set of results, use it to make a specific, testable prediction for a NEW untested value or condition, design a fresh fair test to check that prediction, and explicitly state the reasoning that connects the original data to the prediction. The distinctive skill is turning a one-off experiment into an iterative line of enquiry, while learning that an extrapolated prediction is a claim to be tested, not a proven fact.

activities.title: Predict a new point, then run the test to check it
feedback: If the learner predicts a value already tested, ask 'which value haven't we tried yet? what would you expect there?' to push past the collected points.
If the learner skips the justification, prompt them to complete 'I predict ___ because the results showed ___' before the test runs.
If the prediction is vague ('it'll just go further'), scaffold a specific value or range and a clear fair follow-up set-up.
When a surprising case makes the trend level off, highlight that this is exactly why extrapolated predictions must be tested, not assumed.
If the learner treats the matched prediction as proof the pattern holds forever, discuss that a few points can't guarantee the trend never levels off or reverses.
activities.rationale: The target skill is a cycle — read a trend, commit to a prediction for a new value, then actually test it and compare predicted-vs-measured. An interactive investigation where the learner extends a trend, records reasoning, and then runs a new test can make both the power and the limits of extrapolation concrete. A reasoning field required before the test runs keeps the justification explicit. This proposes an interactive medium as a good fit for showing the predicted-vs-measured moment; a static reference graph can still support the reasoning but cannot show the live follow-up test. Efficacy of the specific mechanism is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to use test results to make predictions to set up further comparative and fair tests.

NGSS SEP 3 (fair tests, controlled variables) and SEP 4 (analyzing and interpreting data to make sense of phenomena and refine solutions) at grades 3-5 together underpin using results to predict and re-test.
learnerActions: Study a graph of results from a completed fair test (e.g. sugar dissolving faster in warmer water, or distance a car rolls from three ramp heights).
Point to the trend in the data in words ('as temperature increased, dissolving got faster') before predicting anything.
Extend the trend line to a temperature/height you never tested and lock in a specific predicted value for that new condition.
Type or say the reasoning: 'I predict ___ BECAUSE the results showed ___' — before any test is run.
Run a fresh fair test at that new value, keeping everything else the same and taking repeat readings, and place the measured point on the graph next to your prediction.
Compare predicted vs measured: discuss when the point lands on your extended line, and what it means when a case makes the trend level off or change instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Good data lets you make an evidence-based prediction for conditions you have not yet tested, but an extrapolated prediction is a claim that must be checked with its own fair test — the pattern may not continue indefinitely, so science is a loop where each result raises the next question.

activities.title: Interpolation vs extrapolation: where is the prediction, and how sure are we?
feedback: If the learner can't distinguish the two, show that interpolation sits inside the measured range while extrapolation reaches past it into untested territory.
If the learner rates an extrapolated prediction as certain, ask what could make the trend level off or reverse past the last tested point.
If a prediction is chosen that merely restates existing data, point out it does not reach beyond the evidence already gathered.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing interpolation from extrapolation and matching predictions to their justifications sharpens the reasoning link and the sense of uncertainty. Selection and sequencing tasks can check whether the learner can identify a well-justified prediction and order the enquiry cycle, but they do not elicit the learner constructing and running their own follow-up test, so they work best as support alongside a hands-on investigation.
learnerActions: On a results graph, mark predictions that fall BETWEEN tested points (interpolation) and predictions that fall BEYOND the tested range (extrapolation).
For each prediction, state whether it is interpolation or extrapolation and rate how certain you can be, explaining why extrapolated predictions carry more uncertainty.
Choose which of several written predictions is best justified by the given data, and explain what makes the others weaker (guess, restated data, or unsupported leap).
Sequence the enquiry cards into the cycle: question → fair test → results → prediction → new fair test.
Say why an extrapolated prediction in particular must be tested rather than assumed.
activities.intendedInsight: Predictions between tested points are generally more secure than predictions beyond the tested range; naming which kind a prediction is tells you how much it needs checking, and an extrapolated prediction especially must be tested because the pattern might not continue.

activities.title: Justify and defend your prediction in dialogue
feedback: If the learner only restates the result, ask them to name an untried value and what they expect there.
If the follow-up design isn't clearly fair, ask what must be kept the same and what will be changed.
If the learner treats the pattern as already proven, discuss that a pattern from a few points might not continue and a further test guards against over-generalising.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue can push the learner to justify a prediction from evidence and defend a follow-up design, exercising the explicit reasoning link that is the core assessed skill. This spoken/written justification complements, rather than replaces, actually running the follow-up test to check the prediction, which may or may not support it.
learnerActions: Answer a mentor's question: 'What does this data make you predict for a value you haven't tried — and why that value?'
Explain how your prediction follows FROM the observed pattern, not from a hunch.
Describe how you would set up the follow-up test so it is fair and actually checks your prediction (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings).
Respond to the challenge: 'What if the trend stops or levels off past a certain point — how would your test reveal that?'
Explain how making an evidence-based prediction differs from simply repeating what you already found.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending the evidence-to-prediction reasoning out loud is the core assessed skill; a prediction without its justification and a fair plan to check it is incomplete.

constraints: Builds on prerequisites: drawing conclusions and making predictions, and independently planning enquiries with variable control (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings).

The prediction must reach a NEW, untested value or condition (interpolation between points or extrapolation beyond the range), not restate a value already measured; the core target skill is extrapolating beyond the tested range and then testing.
The reasoning link must be made explicit in speech or writing ('I predict ___ because the results showed ___'); the justification is the assessed skill, not just the prediction.
The follow-up must be a genuine fair test in its own right, designed to check the specific prediction.

Selection, matching and sequencing tasks can check whether a learner can identify a well-justified prediction and order the enquiry cycle, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner independently constructing a prediction and running their own follow-up test; use them as support, not as the whole objective.
A reference graph can support the reasoning, but on its own it cannot show the learner's own follow-up test or the predicted-vs-measured comparison.
Keep examples honest to real science: an extrapolated pattern may level off or reverse, so do not present the trend as guaranteed to continue indefinitely.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that a static image 'cannot teach' the skill and that '3D adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited standards; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. A fixed graph can still support the reasoning even though it cannot be manipulated or run a live test.

The claim that the interactive loop 'can't be conveyed statically' is a design preference, not an established comparative-efficacy finding from the sources; treat it as a rationale for medium choice, not proof.

The two cited sources support that the standards require using results to predict and set up further fair tests; they do NOT establish that any particular activity format or medium was tested or is most effective.

Independent re-audit: the previously flagged 'optional/required' contradiction in activity 1's reasoning field is resolved — the field is consistently described as required before the test runs. No further learner-facing contradictions or unsupported categorical modality claims were found.

probeDeeper: What exactly would you predict for a height you haven't tried — and why that?
How would you set up the new test so it's fair and actually checks your prediction?
What if the car stopped going further past a certain height — how would your test reveal that? Does the pattern have to continue forever?
How is making a prediction different from just repeating what you already found?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong response uses the pattern in the results to make a specific, testable prediction for a NEW, untried value ('an even higher ramp will roll even further, maybe about X'), and designs a fair follow-up test to check it (new height, everything else kept the same). It explains that the prediction comes FROM the observed pattern, and that a further test is needed because the pattern might not continue (it could level off) — treating the prediction as something to test, not something already proven.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates existing data instead of extrapolating: predicts one of the heights already tested, or just repeats 'higher rolls further' with no new value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'which height haven't we tried yet? what would you expect there?' to push the prediction past the collected points.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The prediction doesn't reach beyond the data already gathered.

errorPatterns.pattern: Pattern treated as proven: 'we already know it, so there's nothing left to check' — sees no need for a follow-up test.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss that a pattern from a few points might not continue; a further test guards against over-generalising.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses the further test as unnecessary because the rule feels certain.

errorPatterns.pattern: Prediction not testable: offers a vague 'it'll go further' with no value and no follow-up design.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold specificity (a value or range) and a fair follow-up set-up that would confirm or refute it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The prediction lacks a specific value/range or any plan for how to check it.

responseLevels.gap: Restates a result already collected, or offers a vague 'it'll go further' with no new value and no follow-up test.
responseLevels.full: Extends the observed pattern into a specific, testable prediction for an untried value, designs a fair follow-up test to check it, and explains that the prediction follows from the pattern yet still needs testing because the pattern might not hold — connecting evidence, inference, and next enquiry.
responseLevels.partial: Makes a prediction for a new value and knows a further test is needed, but the prediction is loosely linked to the pattern, or the follow-up test isn't clearly fair or aimed at checking it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You tested how far a car rolls from three ramp heights and found: the higher the ramp, the further the car rolls. A friend asks, 'So what should we try next?' Using your results, what would you predict for a ramp height you haven't tried yet — and what new test would you set up to check whether your idea holds? Talk me through your thinking.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the idea generates a prediction that goes BEYOND the data (a new, untried value) and sees the need to test it. A child who doesn't merely restates a result already collected, or treats the pattern as proven and sees no reason for a further test. The tell is whether the prediction extends past the evidence and is framed as checkable.
